title: National Council for Adoption v. Blinken
lead: A State Department webpage turned general adoption safeguards into two categorical referral bans. An association first had to establish its members’ injury before the appellate court could decide whether those bans required rulemaking.

actors.name: National Council for Adoption
actors.role: Association of adoption providers challenging guidance on behalf of members.

actors.name: State Department
actors.role: Agency publishing and defending the referral prohibitions.

actors.name: Nightlight Christian Adoptions
actors.role: Member whose president provided specific evidence of past prohibited practices and intended continued referrals.

proceedings: District court struck supplemental standing declarations, dismissed for lack of standing, and denied cross-motions for summary judgment as moot.
Council appealed associational standing, not the separate organizational-standing ruling.
D.C. Circuit on July 9, 2021 reversed, reached the legal classification issue, and remanded with directions to vacate the Guidance.
limits: The ruling did not resolve substantive policy validity, approve particular adoptions, or require all preliminary referrals. State could seek a similar lawful rule after notice and comment. Late declarations were permitted on this record, not by an unlimited reply-stage entitlement.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Website publications define two forbidden preliminary practices
sections.cue: What did the later FAQ permit?
paragraphs: In February 2018, a State Department international-adoption fees webpage declared soft referrals unacceptable and warned of adverse action. Some providers had never encountered that term. A March notice defined two prohibitions: identifying a specific child to prospective parents before the home country found the child eligible for international adoption, even without giving a name; and matching an eligible child with parents lacking an approved home study in a way that removed the child from other families’ consideration, sometimes called holding.

A May FAQ allowed some pre-home-study matching. A provider could not hold a file so that other providers could not refer the child, other parents were discouraged, or authorities could not consider alternatives. The court treated all three publications as the Guidance. It was not a prohibition of every preliminary referral.

Providers faced possible adverse accreditation consequences. The National Council for Adoption, whose members help prospective parents adopt, challenged lack of notice and comment and substantive legality. State said it merely explained policies and regulations dating to 2006.

sections.title: Initial standing evidence prompts supplements and dismissal
sections.cue: Why were the two additional declarations excluded?
paragraphs: State moved to dismiss because the Council had not identified a member harmed by either precise prohibition. Initial member declarations accompanying opposition described matching before home studies; State answered that this did not establish prohibited holding or pre-eligibility referrals.

Under the court’s schedule, both sides also sought summary judgment before dismissal was decided. The Council included two supplemental declarations with its summary-judgment reply. State sought to strike them as late and alternatively challenged sufficiency. The district judge struck them, dismissed for lack of standing, and treated both merits motions as moot.
The Council appealed only associational standing. It did not pursue the separate denial of standing based on injury to the organization itself.

sections.title: Walker restores the declarations and finds associational standing
sections.cue: What made late supplementation permissible here?
paragraphs: Judge Walker, writing with Judge Pillard and Senior Judge Randolph, reviewed standing independently and striking for abuse of discretion. Existing precedent permitted late evidence reinforcing a reasonably substantial earlier showing and making standing patently apparent without prejudice. It did not generally permit first-time standing theories in every reply.

Four circumstances supported admission. The Council reasonably thought its initial substantial showing sufficient. The supplements developed the same theory. Nightlight Christian Adoptions’ president specifically said the member had previously used both banned referrals and would continue appropriate instances but for the prohibition, making injury and causation evident. State showed no prejudice: it attacked the evidence, offered no rebuttal evidence, identified no desired further submission, and did not answer the no-prejudice argument.

Procedural redressability did not demand proof that comments would change policy. With concrete injury established, a possibility that lawful process could prompt reconsideration sufficed. Adoption completion was germane to the Council’s purpose, and neither claims nor requested relief required individual-member participation. Associational standing was established.

sections.title: The panel decides the fully briefed legal merits rather than remanding them unanswered
sections.cue: Why did these bans make new law?
paragraphs: Although threshold reversals ordinarily return merits to the district court, the Council requested immediate decision and State agreed no harm would follow if standing existed. The issue was purely legal, fully briefed, independently reviewed, clear in outcome, and likely to produce another appeal. The panel exercised discretion to resolve it.

A legislative rule has legal effect or exercises delegated power with legal force; an interpretive rule explains a proposition compelled or logically justified by existing law. The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) § 553 exempts genuinely interpretive rules from notice and comment. The Guidance’s prohibitions were enforceable through accreditation, which State did not seriously deny. Its label did not remove those consequences.

State had announced no prior categorical ban and identified no provision compelling these restrictions. On appeal it mainly relied on children’s best interests. Even if a practice often harmed children, an individualized standard did not logically command prohibition in every case. The court’s example of biological relatives almost finished with a home study illustrated why categorical treatment called for rulemaking, not a factual finding that every such referral benefited a child.

sources.pinpoint: Decision to reach merits and rule classification; slip op. 13–16

sections.title: Existing completion deadlines and prior individual actions do not supply the missing rule
sections.cue: What did the court leave open for the agency?
paragraphs: The surrounding framework required eligibility and a home study before completing adoption or placing the child in a home. It did not require both before every preliminary referral. Preliminary action could coexist with later satisfaction of final conditions.

The parties disputed earlier adverse decisions by State or its accreditor involving soft referrals. Even assuming them, State did not argue that those individual decisions compelled a universal prohibition or already created the legal effect now merely explained. They did not bridge the gap between a contextual standard and categorical bans.

On July 9, 2021, the unanimous panel reversed and remanded for an order vacating the Guidance and other consistent action. It did not reach the substantive challenge because the procedural defect sufficed. State could consider a similar policy after notice and comment. The judgment neither compelled an adoption nor made all holding or pre-eligibility referrals lawful, and no separate opinion appeared.

sources.pinpoint: Framework, prior actions, and judgment; slip op. 16–17 & nn.5–6
